summary: First English narrative for Eurybiades' decision at the reconvened council to keep the allied Greek fleet at Salamis rather than withdraw to the Isthmus, written from the case's verified ancient-source facts (Herodotus 7.89 and Book 8; Aeschylus, The Persians 337-383).

narrative.hook: Athens has fallen. You command the allied Greek fleet at Salamis, most of your generals want to sail for the Isthmus, and the Athenian commander has just told you that if you go, his city's ships go too — to Italy.
narrative.short_setup: It is 480 BCE. Xerxes' army has marched through Boeotia into Attica and taken the Athenian acropolis. The Athenians have sent their households to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis itself. After the deaths of Leonidas and his men at Thermopylae, the Peloponnesians have massed at the Isthmus of Corinth and are building a wall across it. The allied fleet lies off Salamis under the Spartan admiral Eurybiades. By Herodotus' count it numbers 378 triremes, and the Athenian ships are by far the most numerous and the most seaworthy among them. The Persian fleet is far larger: Herodotus puts it at 1,207 at the start of the invasion and thinks its losses since have been made good. A first council has already voted to fall back to the Isthmus, and some Peloponnesian commanders were making ready to sail before the vote was even taken. Now, at Themistocles' urging, Eurybiades has called the generals together again.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: Themistocles' argument, as Herodotus gives it, is about geometry. At the Isthmus the fleet would fight in open water, where the enemy's numbers count and the heavier, fewer Greek ships are at a disadvantage. In the narrow strait off Salamis the many cannot all come at the few at once. Staying also protects what withdrawal would abandon: Salamis, where Athenian families are sheltering, along with Megara and Aegina. And sailing to the Isthmus does not move the war away from the Peloponnese; it pulls the Persian army and fleet towards it together. Behind the tactics sits a harder fact. The Athenians supply the core of the fleet, and their commander has said plainly that if it leaves Salamis they will take their households and sail to Siris in Italy. A fleet without the Athenian ships is not a fleet that can fight anywhere.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The majority's case is not cowardice; it is about what happens if things go wrong. If the fleet loses at Salamis, it is trapped on an island, cut off from help, with the land army far away behind its wall. If it loses at the Isthmus, the crews can go ashore onto their own land and keep fighting there. The Peloponnesian commanders' cities, families and army are behind that wall, and the fleet would be beside them rather than stranded in front of a fallen Athens. Most of the generals favour this, the first council has already voted for it, and some contingents are visibly ready to leave. A commander of an allied fleet cannot simply order unwilling allies to stay; keeping the coalition together may mean going where the coalition will go.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Eurybiades changed his mind and resolved to stay and fight at Salamis. Herodotus gives the arguments made at the reconvened council: the tactical case for the narrows, the Corinthian Adeimantus' jibe that Themistocles was a man without a city, Themistocles' reply that so long as Athens had two hundred manned ships it had a city, and the threat to sail for Siris. Herodotus' own judgement is that Eurybiades was moved chiefly by fear that the Athenians would desert if the fleet went to the Isthmus. That is the historian's reading rather than a record of Eurybiades' words, and the speeches themselves are Herodotus' reconstructions. Even so, the decision is presented less as a free tactical choice than as one made under the threat of losing the fleet's largest contingent.
narrative.outcome_story: The decision did not hold. Herodotus says the generals soon argued again and the Peloponnesians were outvoting Themistocles, when he secretly sent his servant Sicinnus to the Persian commanders with word that the Greeks meant to flee. Aeschylus' The Persians also has a messenger report that 'a Hellene, from the Athenian host' brought Xerxes such a message, without naming him. That night the Persian fleet moved to block the exits from the strait and landed troops on the islet of Psyttaleia. Aristides, crossing from Aegina, brought word that the Greeks were surrounded, and a deserting trireme from Tenos confirmed it. The Greeks fought in the strait. Herodotus records that they kept their line while the Persian ships lost their order, and that most of the Persian ships were sunk. Afterwards Xerxes, fearing that the Greeks would sail to the Hellespont and break his bridges, resolved to withdraw.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
The victory makes it tempting to say Eurybiades simply chose right. The decision deserves to be judged on its own terms.

On decision quality: Themistocles' case was strong on what was known at the council. Narrow water really did blunt numerical superiority, withdrawal really did give up Salamis, Megara and Aegina, and the Athenian threat was concrete. The Athenians held the largest contingent, and losing it would have made any later sea battle hopeless. But the majority's case was not foolish. Fighting with no line of retreat is a real risk, and a commander who keeps unwilling allies in place may find they leave anyway. Rated Reasonable: a sound choice, reached under pressure rather than through a clean weighing of options.

On outcome quality: the outcome was good, but the path to it shows how little the council decision settled. The generals wavered again. By Herodotus' account the battle happened in the strait because the Persian fleet closed the exits, and he credits that to a secret message from Themistocles. Aeschylus' version supports the existence of some message, but both are Greek accounts, and the episode should be treated as reported belief. Whatever the cause, the Greeks fought where they did largely because the enemy shut the door. Eurybiades did not have to hold the fleet together by his own authority.

There is also real uncertainty about the alternative. No one can know whether a battle at the Isthmus would have been lost, or whether the Athenians would actually have sailed for Italy. The figures for both fleets differ between the sources and cannot be taken as exact. Herodotus' account of the councils is nearly the only detailed one, written decades later. The fair conclusion is that the case for staying was better on the evidence of the moment. The decisive victory owed a great deal to an enemy choice the council neither foresaw nor controlled.
narrative.decision_principle: When an alliance depends on its strongest member staying, the deciding question may not be which ground is best but which choice keeps the alliance intact — and even a sound decision can need events outside your control to make it stick.
narrative.longform_story:
In 480 BCE the Persian king Xerxes brought his army into Greece. By the time the allied Greek fleet gathered off the island of Salamis, the land war had already gone badly. Leonidas and his men had died at Thermopylae. The Persian army had come through Boeotia, burning Thespiae and Plataea, and was devastating Attica. The Athenians had sent their families across the water to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis. Then news came to the fleet that the acropolis of Athens itself had been taken.

The fleet was commanded by a Spartan, Eurybiades, though Sparta's own squadron was small. Herodotus counts 378 triremes in all, and the largest and best part of them were Athenian. Against them, he says, Xerxes had brought 1,207 ships at the start of the invasion. He judges that the losses since then, to storm and battle, had been made up by new contingents. The tragedian Aeschylus, in his play The Persians, gives a different Greek count of 300 ships plus a chosen ten, and the same 1,207 for Xerxes. The exact numbers are uncertain. The gap between the fleets is not.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesians had done what made sense to them. They had gathered at the Isthmus of Corinth, the narrow neck of land joining their peninsula to the rest of Greece, and were building a wall across it. To many of the fleet's commanders, that was where the fleet belonged too.

At the first council of generals, most of them said so. If they fought at Salamis and lost, they argued, they would be besieged on an island where no one could help them. At the Isthmus, if they lost at sea, they could go ashore to their own lands. When word came that the acropolis had fallen, some Peloponnesian commanders did not wait for a vote; they began making ready to sail. Those who stayed resolved to fight for the Isthmus.

Themistocles of Athens would not accept it. Herodotus says that an Athenian named Mnesiphilus warned him that if the fleet left Salamis it would not fight for any single country at all. Each contingent would go home, and Greece would be lost. Themistocles went to Eurybiades and persuaded him to call the generals together again.

At the second council, Herodotus has Themistocles make the case on tactics. At the Isthmus, he said, they would fight in open water, where heavier and fewer ships are at a disadvantage. They would also give up Salamis, Megara and Aegina, and draw the Persian army towards the Peloponnese along with its fleet. In the narrow strait at Salamis, the few could beat the many. The Corinthian commander Adeimantus answered with contempt: a man without a city, he said, should keep quiet, and Eurybiades should not put such a man's opinion to the vote. Themistocles' reply is the line the episode is remembered for. So long as the Athenians had two hundred manned ships, they had both a city and a land greater than the Corinthians'. Then he turned to Eurybiades with the real threat. If the fleet left, the Athenians would take their households and sail to Siris in Italy, and the allies would remember his words when they had lost them.

It helps to stop here and see the choice as Eurybiades did. Staying meant fighting where the narrows favoured him and keeping the Athenians, who were most of his fleet. It also meant fighting with his back to an island and no road home. Leaving meant a line of retreat and the comfort of the army at the wall. It also meant open water, the loss of Salamis and its neighbours, and quite possibly the loss of the Athenian ships. Neither choice was safe, and the generals around him were split.

Eurybiades chose to stay. Herodotus thinks it was mostly the threat that moved him: the fear that the Athenians would really go. That is the historian's judgement, not a report of the admiral's own words. But it fits the shape of the argument. The tactical case was strong, yet the Athenian threat was what made withdrawal unthinkable.

The decision did not end the matter. Herodotus describes the Peloponnesians growing alarmed again and a new assembly being held. The argument went over the same ground, and Themistocles was being outvoted. At that point, Herodotus says, he slipped out and sent his servant Sicinnus across to the Persian commanders. The message was that the Greeks were frightened and planning to flee, and so divided among themselves that, if the Persians did not let them escape, they would no longer put up a fight. Aeschylus' play carries an echo of the same story: a messenger tells the Persian queen that 'a Hellene, from the Athenian host' came to Xerxes saying the Greeks would try to escape by night. Both accounts are Greek, and they differ in detail. They support the idea that some such message was sent, but the specifics are best treated as what the Greeks came to believe.

That night the Persian fleet moved to close the exits from the strait and landed troops on the small islet of Psyttaleia. Aristides, an Athenian, crossed from Aegina and told the generals they were surrounded. Not all of them believed him until a trireme from Tenos deserted from the Persian side and confirmed it. There was nothing left to debate. The Greeks would fight in the strait because they could no longer leave it.

The battle went as Themistocles had said it could. Herodotus describes the Greeks fighting in order and keeping their line, while the Persian ships fell out of position in the crowded water, and he says most of the Persian ships were sunk. Aeschylus, writing as a Greek imagining the Persian court, presents it as a catastrophe for Xerxes. Afterwards Xerxes, afraid that the Greeks would sail to the Hellespont and break the bridges his army needed to get home, resolved to withdraw. He made some show of preparing to fight again and sent a messenger to Persia with the news.

It would be easy to tell this as the story of a wise admiral making the right call. The record is messier and more instructive. The case for staying was the better one on what the council knew. But Eurybiades reached it under threat, his allies did not accept it, and the battle happened in the narrows largely because the enemy came in and shut the door. The alternative cannot be tested. No one knows whether a battle at the Isthmus would have been lost, or whether the Athenians would really have sailed for Italy. What can be said is that the decision was sound, the victory was real, and the first did not by itself produce the second.
